item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q025_classification_as_evolutionary_hypothesis","answer":"It should be classified as a new superfamily in the existing fold, not as a new family of an old superfamily and not as a new fold. At SCOPe release 2.08, for example, SCCS a is the All alpha proteins class, a.4 is the DNA/RNA-binding 3-helical bundle fold, and a.4.1 is the Homeodomain-like superfamily; those ranks illustrate the logic: class records broad secondary-structure composition, fold records the same major secondary structures in the same arrangement and topology, superfamily is the level at which SCOPe asserts probable common ancestry, and family is an even closer homologous grouping inside a superfamily. A new family under an existing superfamily would therefore make too strong an evolutionary claim here: it would say the new domain is homologous to that superfamily but not close enough for an existing family. A new superfamily under the already recognized fold makes the narrower claim that the domain has the fold-level structural topology while homology to every current superfamily in that fold is absent or unconvincing. A new fold would make a different structural claim, namely that the core topology is not represented by any existing fold, so mere lack of superfamily-level homology is not enough to justify it. Because a fold can contain analogous, nonhomologous superfamilies, fold resemblance alone should not be used to transfer ancestry, detailed function, exact active-site equivalence, or choose a close comparative-model template as if the proteins were homologs; those require additional evidence such as sequence profiles, conserved motifs, oligomeric and ligand-binding context, and structure comparisons strong enough to support a common-ancestry hypothesis.","evidence_used":["mcp__scope.get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.4; /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.4/parents","mcp__scope.get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.4.1; /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/a.4.1/parents"]}]}
